text: Your manager asks you to sketch the data model for a new custom application: Equipment Request, used when an employee needs a one-off piece of hardware that isn't in the standard new-hire kit — a second monitor, a graphics tablet, a specialized dock. Before anyone opens Studio or touches System Definition and Tables, you're asked to think through the design on paper. This is exactly the kind of planning conversation a real ServiceNow admin has before building anything at all.

First, what should this table extend? A brand-new table built on nothing would have to reinvent state, assignment_group, priority, and approval tracking from scratch. Cmdb_ci is the wrong fit entirely — an equipment request isn't a configuration item, it's a request for one. The right answer is task. An Equipment Request needs a lifecycle, routing to an assignment group, and plausibly approval tracking — exactly the shared behavior Lesson 11 showed living on task.

Extending task means this new table inherits state, short_description, assignment_group, and priority for free, the same way incident and problem do, and only needs to add fields specific to an equipment request on top. Next, what reference fields does it need? Requested_for, pointing to sys_user, identifies which employee the equipment is for, since an admin might submit the request on someone else's behalf — the requester and the recipient aren't always the same person.

Equipment_item, the second reference field, points to a catalog-style table listing the specific hardware items available to request, so the request stores a clean pointer to exactly which item was chosen, rather than a free-text description someone has to interpret later. Both fields follow the exact pattern from Lesson 13 — a field that displays a readable value but stores a sys_id, with auto-complete and a preview icon built in for free.

Laid out for review: Equipment Request extends task, inheriting lifecycle and routing behavior, then adds requested_for and equipment_item as its own reference fields on top. Nothing here required opening the platform — fixing a wrong extends-table choice after records already exist is far more disruptive than getting it right on paper first. Next up: Chapter 4 begins with the dictionary, and exactly what it controls.
